title: Factorising a difference of two squares
keyIdea: Expressions of the form a² − b² factorise as (a + b)(a − b). Both terms must be perfect squares with a minus between them. Handle coefficients such as 9x² − 25 as (3x + 5)(3x − 5). Sums like x² + 49 do not use this pattern over the reals.
familyTip: Ask: factorise x² − 64. Then: why does x² + 49 not work the same way?

visual.caption: Difference-of-squares idea or mix-up? Drag each clue, or tap it then a box.

items: need two squares and a minus

lab.caption: Flagship lab: reveal a²−b²=(a+b)(a−b), build (x+7)(x−7), factorise 9x²−25, reject x²+49, catch mix-ups, then challenge.

kid: A difference of two squares is one square take away another square, like a² − b². It factorises as (a + b)(a − b).
Example: x² − 49 is x² − 7², so (x + 7)(x − 7). Expand to check: the middle terms cancel and you get back x² − 49.
With coefficients, take square roots of both square terms. 9x² − 25 is (3x)² − 5², so (3x + 5)(3x − 5).
A sum of squares such as x² + 49 does not factorise with this pattern over the real numbers. You need the minus.
adult: Ages 14 to 16. GCSE Algebra / CCSS A-SSE.2: factorise a² − b² including simple coefficients. Separate from the geometric perfect-squares area demo.

Words: difference of two squares, factorise, perfect square, coefficient, expand, sum of squares. Common mistakes: writing (a − b)² for a² − b²; treating x² + n as a difference; taking √(9x²) as 9x; dropping one bracket.
In the lab the learner reveals the identity, marks both brackets for x² − 49, factorises 9x² − 25, rejects the sum, spots the (a − b)² myth, and orders the method.

practice.hint: One sum bracket and one difference bracket.
practice.explain: The identity is a² − b² = (a + b)(a − b). A single squared bracket is a different expansion.

practice.hint: Square each number, then subtract. Same as (a+b)(a−b).
Take the square root of each square term, including the coefficient on x.
The constant term is a squared.
practice.explain: (x + {a})(x − {a}) = x² − {a}², so the subtracted number is {=a*a}.

practice.hint: Compare (a − b)² with the true difference-of-squares identity.
practice.explain: (a − b)² expands to a² − 2ab + b², not a difference of squares.
